name: Shrugs / trap training

lead: Shrugs raise the shoulders against weight to train the upper trapezius. In looksmaxxing talk, bigger traps fill the base of the neck and make it look thicker, with a fuller neck and shoulder line.

Resistance on shoulder elevation works the upper trapezius. Electromyography studies have measured muscle activation during neck and shoulder strengthening exercises, including in women with chronic neck muscle pain and in novices during a shoulder resistance bout. None of this research addresses how the neck looks.

paras: People add shrugs with dumbbells, barbells or machines to upper-body routines, and trap size builds over months like other muscle training.
No harms are documented in the available sources. Height-gain claims from shrugs have not been studied.

web.title: Europe PMC: upper trapezius shrug EMG studies

angle.text: Users train shrugs to build the upper trapezius, which fills the base of the neck and makes the neck and shoulder line look thicker. Research on shrugs covers muscle activation during the exercise.

lead: Shrugs and trapezius training are resistance exercises in which the shoulders are raised against a load to build the upper trapezius, the superficial muscle that runs from the base of the skull and neck out toward the shoulders [1]. People train it to give the neck and upper back a thicker, more developed look: a larger upper trapezius fills the slope between neck and shoulder, which lifters associate with a more powerful, broader-looking frame [2].

The appearance chain is direct and mechanical. Loaded shoulder elevation is the exercise most associated with the upper fibres, regular resistance training is the general route to muscle growth, and the upper trapezius is one of the few back muscles visible from the front and side as part of the neck and shoulder line [1][1][3]. Variants include barbell, dumbbell, machine and behind-the-neck shrugs, and pulling movements such as hang cleans that also load the upper fibres [1][4].

Published research on shrug-type exercises concerns muscle activation, soreness and neck-pain rehabilitation rather than cosmetic outcomes. Electromyography studies in healthy volunteers and in women with chronic neck pain identify the shrug as a high-activation exercise for the upper trapezius [2][5]. In looksmaxxing forums, traps appear in neck, posture and physique threads and, in one thread, in a question about height [6][7].
infobox: EMG and rehabilitation studies; no appearance studies

paras: The trapezius is a large, paired, trapezium-shaped muscle of the back, historically called the cucullaris. It has three functional parts. The upper (descending) fibres run from the base of the skull, the nuchal ligament and the C7 vertebra to the outer collarbone and support the weight of the arm. The middle fibres retract the scapula, and the lower fibres, arising from T4 to T12, depress and rotate it [1][1].

The accessory nerve supplies motor control. Together the upper and lower fibres rotate the scapula upward, helping lift the arm above 90 degrees, and when the shoulder blades are stable both sides contracting together can extend the neck [1]. Because the muscle is superficial, its size shows in the line of the neck and shoulders, and trapezius palsy is associated with a drooping shoulder, which illustrates its role in shoulder posture [1][1].

Anatomical references map exercises to regions of the muscle: shoulder shrugs and hang cleans train the upper fibres, neck extension works the uppermost area, pulling the shoulder blades together develops the middle fibres and drawing them downward with straight arms works the lower fibres [1]. In a shrug, weights held in the hands are lifted by raising the shoulders toward the ears without rolling them [4].

Variants include barbell, dumbbell and machine shrugs, as well as single-arm versions. The Hise shrug, named for Joseph Curtis Hise, a figure of the 1930s who died in 1972, holds a barbell behind the neck [4]. Olympic-lift derivatives such as hang cleans and pulls load the traps as part of a whole-body movement; an exploratory electromyography study of 27 weightlifters compared trapezius activity in hang power cleans, snatches and pulls at several percentages of maximum, finding differences between lift variations at some intensities [5].

Muscle hypertrophy is generally attributed to mechanical tension on the muscle, which activates mechanosensitive pathways including mTOR and raises muscle protein synthesis. Training frequency, intensity and total volume all affect growth, and increasing them gradually produces gains [3]. Neural adaptations appear first and measurable growth follows [3].

Heritable factors matter: one estimate puts about 53 percent of the variance in lean body mass as heritable, and testosterone is a major driver of the sex difference in muscle mass [3]. A meta-analysis cited in Wikipedia's account found that protein intake up to about 1.6 g per kg of body weight per day supported strength and size gains, with no added hypertrophy benefit reported above about 1.8 g/kg [3].

Rehabilitation literature discusses the ratio of upper to lower trapezius activity, because the upper fibres tend to dominate in many shoulder exercises. A Brazilian Journal of Physical Therapy review describes how to target each trapezius region selectively [5]. In a 2022 study of university archers, a twelve-week programme centred on the lower trapezius changed the upper-to-lower ratio from 2.2 to 1.1 and improved shooting scores in the exercise group [5]. Lifters who care about neck and back appearance often pair shrugs with rowing and pulling movements for the middle and lower fibres; the sources do not test this for looks.

A 2003 surface electromyography study of 30 healthy subjects in the Journal of Orthopaedic and Sports Physical Therapy compared exercises for the trapezius and serratus anterior and reported that the unilateral shoulder shrug produced the greatest activity in the upper trapezius [5].

A physical therapy randomized trial used surface electromyography to measure muscle activity in 12 women aged 30 to 60 with chronic trapezius myalgia during lateral raises, upright rows, shrugs, one-arm rows and reverse flys. Activation of the trapezius was highest during the shrug, at about 102 percent of a maximal voluntary static contraction, followed by lateral raises at about 97 percent and upright rows at about 85 percent [2].

A separate study evaluated muscle activity across a standardized shoulder resistance session in novice trainees [8]. A randomized trial in 20 healthy women compared 10 minutes of massage with 10 minutes of shrugs against elastic resistance for relieving soreness 48 hours after eccentric upper-trapezius work [9]. A manual therapy study compared pressure pain thresholds in the trapezius region in young people with and without a depressed scapula [10]. None of these assessed changes in neck appearance.

One looksmax.org poster reported apparent height gain of about half a centimetre after heavy shrugs and asked whether it was real growth or improved posture [6]. The excerpt available does not include replies, and no study has measured height change from shrugs.

Lifters planning aesthetics-focused routines also discuss barbell and dumbbell-only programs built on compound lifts such as squats, bench press, overhead press and deadlifts, plus lateral raises, which fit the broader goal of a wider, fuller upper body [7].

The sources describe shrugs as a low-complexity exercise, and the studies above found them used in rehabilitation settings for neck pain. The Hise shrug's behind-the-neck bar position is a named variant [4]. Neck and shoulder pain populations in the studies were supervised in research or therapy contexts [2][9].

No studies found on shrugs for cosmetic neck thickness or height. Electromyography studies of shoulder and neck exercises exist in pain rehabilitation, healthy-volunteer and novice training populations [2][8][5].
